item.title: Starlink 'Community Site' Program Teases Hourly, Weekly Internet Passes (2 minute read)
item.description: Starlink plans to offer hourly, daily, and weekly passes for its satellite internet service. The company is recruiting 'hosts' to sell passes to interested consumers. Pricing details have yet to be released. Starlink will take care of payments, user access, and connectivity while the hosts focus on setting up their sites and earning from connections.

item.title: Why Muse May Never Need Ads (13 minute read)
item.description: Meta is one of the very few companies that can monetize a personal agent through advertising without ever showing an ad inside the agent itself. The company can keep ads out of the Muse app and still get paid for it on Facebook and Instagram. Every Muse errand can be an incremental signal. Meta can indirectly monetize Muse until enough demand has been aggregated for it to start with direct monetization.

item.title: World's first enhanced geothermal power plant completed in just 23 months (2 minute read)
item.description: Fervo Energy has started selling electricity from its Cape Station geothermal power plant. It is the first enhanced geothermal company to reach a key commercial milestone. The entire site has the potential to generate as much as 4 gigawatts of electricity. The first block at the site took 23 months to complete - Fervo aims to complete future blocks in as little as 18 months.

item.title: With PRIMA, NASA will try to build a billion-dollar space telescope in record time (6 minute read)
item.description: NASA's Probe Explorers are a new line of observatories intended to do more science for less money. The project aims to seek a better balance between the smaller Explorer missions and multibillion-dollar flagships. NASA announced on Wednesday it was moving forward with the first of the Explorers, PRIMA (Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics). PRIMA will observe the universe in faint, far-infrared light in a range of wavelengths between 24 and 235 micrometers. NASA intends to launch the telescope in 2033.

item.title: Pi Durable (33 minute read)
item.description: Pi Durable is an experimental package built specifically for long-running, durable, and malleable agents that can run anywhere. It can run anywhere, can be reached from different surfaces, supports infinitely long conversations, survives catastrophic internal and external failures, and lets multiple humans steer the same agents. It is a framework for building any agentic application, including coding agents.

item.title: RoR creator sparks new “death of coding by hand” debate (15 minute read)
item.description: David Heinemeier Hansson, the creator of Ruby on Rails, recently announced that 37signals, a company known for its software craft, was done with writing code by hand. The maturation of AI tools has made it possible for the company to embrace a future where coding by hand is almost entirely absent. AI creates new business models and revenue streams and disrupts traditional software. Companies are now investing in innovation and are willing to pay top-of-market for software engineers who can help them build AI products or become AI-native.

item.title: Xbox's Millennial CEO Isn't Playing Around (13 minute read)
item.description: Asha Sharma, the 38-year-old chief executive of Microsoft's Xbox division, wants Xbox properties to entertain a billion people. This means opening untapped markets in Africa, Latin America, and South Asia by using cloud computing technology to run games on computers and smartphones. Another pillar of her strategy is to reinvest in Minecraft as a competitor to Roblox. Leaders at the company describe the future of its consoles as embodying that idea.

item.title: Apple Is Finally Ready to Enter Its Next Big Category: the Smart Home (8 minute read)
item.description: Apple is preparing to launch several smart home devices on October 13. The company plans to ship a smart-home hub, an updated HomePod mini, and a new TV set-top box. The company is developing a broader smart-home ecosystem that expands on HomeKit software and supports new categories of connected products. It is also working with third-party manufacturers on devices designed for the Siri AI home platform.

item.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Argon AI model, but you can't use it yet (3 minute read)
item.description: Google's Gemini 4 Argon model offers industry-leading performance in coding, knowledge work, and cybersecurity. Google's engineers are already using the model extensively, and Argon-powered agents have been working to migrate C/C++ codebases to Rust across Google. The model supports an output limit of 1 million tokens. It will be priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens for a limited time. The model is still in limited testing, and there is no timeline for when it will be available to enterprise and consumer customers.

item.title: Google figures out how to watermark AI-designed proteins (11 minute read)
item.description: The DeepMind team at Google has developed a technique that can create watermarks on protein sequences without compromising the protein's function. The watermark is impossible to remove and can survive basic exporting, resizing, and other editing. The system could be used to give DNA synthesizers greater confidence in their sources.

item.title: Most powerful obesity drug yet: People lost up to 25% of weight in trial (5 minute read)
item.description: Late-stage clinical trial data on the obesity drug retatrutide showed an average loss of 25% of body weight after 90 weeks. More than a third of the participants taking the drug in the trial lost 30% or more of their weight. The drug also helped reduce knee pain and sleep apnea events, and it improved cardiometabolic measurements across the board. At the start of the trial, more than a third of trial participants had prediabetes - the condition had resolved in more than 90% of those participants by the end.

Being able to explain why you are shipping something will help you explain or fix it if it breaks later. AI can do the work - writing why is where you find out whether you understand what you are shipping.

item.title: Tech CEOs Privately Questioned Amodei for Sounding AI Alarm Bells (7 minute read)
item.description: AI chief executives gathered with Trump at the White House on Tuesday to discuss a statement of principles to keep AI models safe. Behind the scenes, the executives questioned Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about his warnings about the dangers of AI, asking why he was being so extreme in public about the capabilities of AI models and the risks they pose. Amodei told them it was important to be honest with the public about model capabilities and not play down risks. He believes that safety is possible if the industry and administration work together.

item.title: Apple's New CEO Seeks to Make Company Run Faster and Leaner (7 minute read)
item.description: Apple CEO John Ternus is moving to overhaul the company to accelerate product development, broaden its range of devices, and create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering. Early ideas under consideration include relying less on traditional spring and fall product release schedules and eliminating some middle-management positions. Ternus has indicated that the company should introduce products more quickly and become more experimental to remain competitive in the AI era. He is seeking new sources of revenue and ways to generate more money from existing products.

item.title: NASA has a Dragon dilemma, and there appear to be no good answers (7 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX has made it clear to NASA that it no longer wishes to fly its Crew Dragon spacecraft, or the Falcon 9 rocket, on missions to low-Earth orbit. The company has agreed to support the International Space Station until 2030, but it intends to retire the spacecraft after that. SpaceX has told companies developing private space stations for low-Earth orbit that they cannot order Crew Dragon missions for their habitats. The company has more than fulfilled its contract obligations to NASA, so it is unlikely that the agency can compel SpaceX to keep flying Dragon.

item.title: Pilotless plane flies over Wichita, putting the future of aviation on display (2 minute read)
item.description: Joby Aviation recently flew its autonomous aircraft over Wichita. The company has developed a base system that can function in any aircraft. The plane used in the demonstration was a Cessna 208 Caravan that had been retrofitted with Joby's technology. Joby plans to start using the autonomous plane in emergency and cargo transport operations over the next few years, but its end goal is to make it a safe, viable transportation option.

item.title: Data is the application (6 minute read)
item.description: AI makes it possible to build faster than ever. However, none of that speed applies to the data. Lose the data that users give you, and you have to start all over again. Let agents iterate over the code, but leave the data to humans.

item.title: When AI Models Hurt People, the Labs Should Pay (18 minute read)
item.description: Tech's red line has always been liability. As a technology matures, society sets more legal regimes, either through explicit regulation or case law. Previous technology waves have shown that industries can survive paying for the harms they cause. One would have to question the societal benefits of an industry if paying for the people it harms or kills is enough to kill the industry.

While the best use of Meta's compute will be its first-party products, an enterprise platform as a 'second' customer makes sense. If Meta underbuilds and can't serve the product it just found product-market fit for, users will drift to competing AI agents/products.

item.title: OpenAI Scraps Release of New AI Model Over Safety Concerns (6 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI is scrapping the release of GPT-6.1 Astra due to safety concerns. The company had aimed to launch the model in October, but the model performed poorly on tests measuring alignment compared to its predecessor. GPT-6.1 Astra showed higher levels of deception, and it would push ahead on tasks without asking users for permission. It would also reach for external tools and services even if it might be unsafe. OpenAI says it is working to investigate a range of agent security incidents and address the safety issues underneath them.

item.title: SpaceX's Starship Makes It to Orbit for the First Time, but Returns to Earth Early (8 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX's Starship circled Earth on Monday. The spacecraft had to return to Earth after less than two orbits instead of the planned six because of engine problems that occurred during liftoff. The Starship spacecraft splashed down with a fiery explosion in the North Pacific near Hawaii before noon. Reaching orbit is a key milestone towards SpaceX's goal of eventually sending people to Mars as well as NASA's plans to send astronauts back to the moon.

The craft has now moved to the parts that decide whether the code deserves to be trusted.

item.title: OpenAI Pauses Training Most Capable Models After Sandbox Escape (3 minute read)
item.description: OpenAI claims one of its agentic AI systems trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external third-party chatbot. The agent apparently exploited a gap to reach the public internet to send 20 queries to an unnamed, third-party chatbot service. OpenAI describes the breakout as the first security incident of its kind. The company has stopped training the model, but said it provided an important signal about where to focus the next phase of work.

item.title: Meta's VR Glasses Are What the Apple Vision Pro Should Have Been (16 minute read)

This article offers a look at what the new Meta VR Glasses experience is like compared to the Vision Pro. For a device that won't launch until next Spring, the experience is surprisingly refined, and the glasses improve on the Vision Pro in several ways.

item.title: Waymo's Latest Safety Numbers Sure Make Human Drivers Look Bad (3 minute read)
item.description: Waymo reports 82% fewer injury-causing crashes than human drivers. The company has released data collected from over 270 million miles of fully autonomous driving. Waymo cars were involved in 95% fewer collisions that caused serious injury or worse, and there were 93% fewer pedestrian incidents that resulted in injuries compared to human drivers. While the company's data only measure the five metropolitan areas where it operated during the study period, it shows that the company's driverless robotaxis crash far less frequently than humans.

item.title: SpaceX's Starship Is Set to Make Its First Orbital Flight (8 minute read)
item.description: SpaceX is aiming to reach orbit on Starship's 14th test flight. The test flight is scheduled for Monday at around 8 AM ET, with SpaceX providing live coverage of the event on its website. Achieving orbital flight will allow Starship to deploy satellites and travel to more distant destinations. SpaceX will not try to catch the two rocket stages during the test - the booster will make a simulated landing in the Gulf of Mexico, and the upper stage will simulate a landing in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile.

item.title: S3 Is the Future, S3 Is the Past (5 minute read)
item.description: Since S3's release 20 years ago, SSD prices have dropped steadily, and the gap between SSD and disk has narrowed to roughly 3x. The industry is codifying architectural patterns that exist to work around limitations that SSD storage doesn't have. Cloud providers have no incentive to disrupt a model that serves them well, so developers need to build the infrastructure primitives themselves.

item.title: Google's first Suncatcher orbital data center test launches October 1 (3 minute read)
item.description: Project Suncatcher is a moonshot effort by Google to design orbital AI data centers. Its first experimental satellite will launch on October 1. Its aim will be to validate Google's vision for a constellation of AI satellites. The satellite, about the size of a refrigerator, has four custom TPU AI accelerators and solar panels that supply about one kilowatt of power. It will serve as a test of several technologies over its few months of operation.

item.title: Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin Is Fueled With $30 Billion of His Fortune (4 minute read)
item.description: Jeff Bezos has invested $30 billion in Blue Origin since its founding in 2000. The commitment has helped Blue Origin become a large space company with around 15,000 employees and an ambitious growth plan. Blue Origin recently raised capital from outside investors for the first time. The company expects to produce about $1.4 billion in revenue this year, growing that number to more than $30 billion in 2030.

item.title: There's a new way to break RSA that's faster than anything we've seen before (5 minute read)
item.description: Researchers have discovered a novel method that uses classical computing to reduce the current RSA security level to an unacceptably low threshold. The practical risk is limited, but still significant. Widely used RSA implementations are also safe. The technology involves signature forgery and reduces the required computing resources by orders of magnitude.

item.title: Waymo is scaling fast: Here's what the fleet data shows (4 minute read)
item.description: Waymo appears to be concentrating its efforts in just two states. 80% of its roughly 4,000 robotaxis are in California and Texas. Waymo's fleet has grown by nearly half in the past three weeks in Texas. The company's remaining 800 or so vehicles are spread across cities in other states, including Arizona and Florida. A growing number of the vehicles in Waymo's fleet are Chinese-built minivans.

item.title: A new trend of CPU shortages (10 minute read)
item.description: Many companies are struggling to source CPUs. CPU spot pricing has disappeared because there's no longer any lack of demand for CPUs. It's now nearly impossible to get CPUs on spot instances without long-running connections with cloud providers. Reserving specific CPUs now needs to be done months in advance. Cloud providers will even turn down certain reservations because they don't have enough CPUs or the right type of CPUs.

item.title: Thinking in Systems, Shipping in Loops (3 minute read)
item.description: AI has removed the typing from software engineering but left the system design. What's left is designing the loop that decides whether the output is right. Great system design is defined by resilience, self-organization, and hierarchy. Resilience is AI checking its own work, self-organization is the loop learning, and hierarchy is the layering of skills, tools, and sandboxes into composable components that are reused once verified to work.

item.title: The Specter Of Neuralese (20 minute read)
item.description: Neuralese recurrence is a hypothetical technology that would allow AIs to think dangerous thoughts without getting detected. OpenAI's new Astra model uses a reasoning technique called recurrent depth that makes the model's chain of thought more difficult to monitor by allowing it to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models. There is an emerging taboo on creating dangerous neuralese AIs. It is unclear whether OpenAI broke that taboo, as a clear line has yet to be drawn.

item.title: Zuckerberg's ‘Tamagotchi-Like' AI Could Be Meta's iPod Moment (6 minute read)
item.description: Meta announced a Tamagotchi-like pendant for interacting with its Muse personal agent on Wednesday. The device, expected to be out in time for Christmas, features a customizable character at the center of the screen. It can be worn with a wrist strap, carried in a pocket, or attached to a bag or keychain with a lanyard. The devices can interact with each other when placed near each other. Muse Charm could open up new streams of revenue that could eclipse the company's advertising business.

item.title: Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats (11 minute read)
item.description: Claude autonomously discovered a novel enzyme system that is associated with an array of DNA repeats. The system's function is still unknown, but it is programmable and can perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA. It is based on a reverse transcriptase previously known to science, but Claude appears to be the first to notice the system's defining features - an associated array of non-coding DNA sequences and an additional accessory protein of unknown function.

item.title: Meta Launches Lightweight $1,299 VR Headset That Looks Like Glasses (5 minute read)
item.description: Meta has launched the Meta VR Glasses at $1,299. The device has many of the same features as Meta's existing Quest headsets. Its processor, cooling fan, battery, and other computing components are housed in an external pack. At about 100 grams, the device is roughly one-sixth the weight of Apple's Vision Pro.

item.title: Grail's Multi-Cancer Blood Test Gets FDA Committee Vote for Premarket Approval (2 minute read)
item.description: Grail has received a favorable vote from an FDA panel regarding premarket approval for its multi-cancer early detection test. The test is designed to detect cancer-specific methylation patterns and, if detected, predict the cancer signal origin with high accuracy to help guide diagnostic evaluation. While the FDA isn't bound to the committee's decision, it takes them into consideration when making the final regulatory decision. It is expected to make its final ruling on the test's premarket approval in the coming months.

item.title: China puts AI compute into orbit with Supercomputing-1 satellite — onboard processing aims to cut Earth-observation data processing from hours to minutes (2 minute read)
item.description: China has launched nine satellites into orbit as part of a push to put AI computing in space. The Supercomputing-1 satellite that launched on the mission is designed to capture and process Earth-observation data in orbit instead of sending data back to terrestrial data centers. It features both a high-res optical payload and an image-processing AI computer. Local processing will cut cross-regional data processing times from hours to minutes.

item.title: A Redistribution of Code Ownership (7 minute read)
item.description: Product managers and designers used to have to think through a great deal ahead of time because the build was a larger investment, and the people paying for it wanted to know what they were getting before they committed. Agent coding changes the process so that nobody has to hold the whole vision in their head and transfer it losslessly to someone else. Engineers have historically owned code out of necessity, but AI enables a model of ownership and collaboration that is distributed a little more evenly.

item.title: How we made claude.ai 3x faster in two weeks (15 minute read)
item.description: Anthropic made the core user experience of claude.ai and the Claude desktop app about 3x faster during a two-week sprint in August. Time to a typeable page on a fresh load of claude.ai went from 3.1 seconds to 0.55 seconds, starting a new Claude Code session went from 0.8 seconds to 0.3 seconds, and loading a Claude Cowork cloud session went from 2.6 seconds to 0.73 seconds. The optimizations will likely save an estimated tens of thousands of user-hours of waiting every day. This post covers what the Claude team shipped, how they measured it, and the loop they built with Claude to do it safely.

item.title: Meta Muse is People (4 minute read)
item.description: Meta has been testing a human concierge for its Muse AI personal assistant. Human contractors are quietly handling some of the phone calls placed via the digital agent. The Muse agent is designed to autonomously perform tasks like sending emails, shopping, and booking travel on a person's behalf. The phone-calling feature allows users to tell the agent to dial phone numbers for businesses in the US and talk with people to handle errands like booking haircuts, checking whether a store has an item in stock, or getting quotes from different contractors.
